There weren't only three hundred Spartans at Thermopylae. There were also about 2,000 allied troops, specifically, Thespians (no, not actors) who fought with a ferocity and skill second only to the Spartans themselves, and Arcadians too. And there were more Spartans as well. The 300 were backed about two-for-one by their squires and helots (slaves) who carried their goods. But by the third day, attrition by reason of casualties had worn down the Spartan line too far. Consequently, the squires -- teenage boys for the most part -- moved up to fill their fallen lords' places. So too did the Spartan helots -- their slaves, voluntarily, taking on Spartan red and dying alongside their masters even though they had no reason to remain.

The legend of the three hundred comes from what Leonidas did on the third day of the battle. Knowing that Xerxes' Immortals had taken the goat trail around behind the Spartan position, Leonidas ordered all his allies to quit the field, intending only to hold the Persians for a few hours so his allies could get clear or at least get a good headstart on the Persians' advance. Even then the Thespians refused the order and died alongside the Spartans in the final bloody hour.

Gates of Fire is essentially the story of Xeones, one of the Spartan helots, who survives his wounds long enough to narrate the story of his people to the fascinated Xerxes as the Persian invasion of the Peloppenese continues.

In terms of tone, it's pretty heavy on detail, light on melodrama. Basically the opposite of the film 300, though 300 certainly seems to get the spirit of the event right. David Gemmell (Legend, Lion of Macedon) really liked it, probably because the style is very similar to his own books: not a hell of a lot of time for deep passionate sobs or beating the breast over lost lovers; the emotion is squeezed out of the characters in the sweat of battle, it's ripped from men as spears, swords, and axes tear them open.

Pressfield seems to have thoroughly researched his material. He gives you a strong vision of Greek culture of the time, and Spartan culture in particular. It's not a pretty period in history: Xeones at one point is a thief of about 10 or 11 years old and is crucified -- literally -- by a farmer when he's caught stealing. The Spartan agoge, the Spartan training school, is similarly brutal: for infractions, students are literally beaten across the back with thumb-thick wooden rods until they collapse. One character is killed during this process.

Pressfield -- an ex-Marine -- gets the smells, the sweat, and the emotions that run through soldiers generally. But he also portrays clearly how those emotions were handled by the Spartans. For example, people often tremble after battle. Today we'd describe it as adrenaline, but, contrary to what you'd expect, the Spartans didn't think of that trembling as shameful at all. They called it fear-shedding, getting rid of fear after a fight is over, and as matter of fact as taking a big shit after a big meal. That's because they had a fascinating, quasi-medical idea about fear itself: one of the big subjects in Spartan training was training the individual to identify where fear rose in the body and what exercises combated it. Many other surprises await anyone who's only got a casual, Wikipedia knowledge of the battle. Did you think Gerard Butler as Leonidas was unrealistic? Try the idea that Leonidas was sixty fucking years old when he led his men to the Hot Gates, and was fighting consistently all through the three days of the battle. Spartan culture is not glorified in this book, but neither is there any authorial tut-tutting over what the Spartans do, either. It is simply representing how they lived, and it's moving at times for that very reason.

There is also a spiritual aspect to the book, though those sorts of things are better left unreported. You are certainly invited to consider across the book why Xeones, a slave, wants to stand and die at Thermopylae so much. The book's style is not high falutin' eloquence ... but I realise as I sit here that this was probably intentional by Pressfield. The story is the account of a soldier in the Spartan army, not a bloody philosopher. It's heavy on detail and it's full of spirit. It's on the reading list for the Marine Academy, so I understand. Take what you will from that, and have a read of this impressive book.

The only drawback I had to the whole experience was the miserly way my paperback had been produced. The bastards wanted to save the fucking dollars on paper, so they made the page margins too wide, meaning the text wound up printed too close in to the book's spine. The result being you just about have to tear the book in half to read the full lines comfortably. Cheap pricks.
